newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's retired Katanga rebels now back Kabila.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's retired Katanga rebels now back Kabila.

text.p: Katangan gendarmes, Africa's most peripatetic fighting force, are ready to switch sides again and back Laurent Kabila, leader of Zaire's advancing rebels.
Officers from the long-exiled force, which fought for the independence of Shaba province in the 1960s and 1970s, said on Friday they now supported the rebels.

"We will help Kabila come here, we are all behind him now," one senior officer, who declined to be named, said in Lubumbashi. In theory the gendarmes are on the same side as President Mobutu Sese Seko's ragged army.
Zaire's second city is the capital of copper-rich Shaba, called Katanga before President Mobutu Sese Seko renamed it.
"We are Katangan and Kabila is Katangan, it would be hard for us to fight our own brothers."
The Katangan gendarmes, forced into exile in neighbouring Angola after failed secession attempts in the 1960s, are best known for two incursions into Shaba in 1977 and 1978.
In 1978 they occupied the copper-mining town of Kolwezi, where some of the 2,000 Belgian residents were massacred in a conflict that ended when French troops helped Mobutu regain control.
The massacre sent shudders sround the world and led to the abandonment of major foreign investments in Shaba's mines.
The legendary "gendarmes Katangais" were first recruited by the late Katangan leader Moise Tshombe and Belgian interests who tried to secede after independence from Belgium in 1960.
The bid failed and for 30 years the gendarmes and their offspring were Africa's supreme military opportunists, taking their skills to Angola and renting them out periodically in far-flung conflicts.

In 1990, around half of some 15,000 gendarmes -- by now including sons of the original force and new recruits -- accepted Mobutu's offer to come home and join in the transition to democracy which he has now stretched out for seven years.
The other half mistrusted him and stayed in exile. Some are fighting already with Kabila, who says he opposes secession.
Diplomats in the Angolan capital Luanda told Reuters on March 14 the government was sending exiled Katangese back home to join in the fight to overthrow Mobutu.

"The Angolan government may be saying publicly they do not have any troops in Zaire but the fact is they are flying transport planes with these Katangese aboard out of bases around Luanda to Zaire," an African diplomat said.
"There are a number of Angolan military units made up entirely of Katangese. These are the ones who have been sent to help out the rebels," said another.
Angola's government has every reason to get back at Mobutu for supporting Jonas Savimbi's UNITA rebels during the 30-year civil war.
There are repeated but unconfirmed reports that thousands of UNITA veterans have also entered Shaba from Angola to help Mobutu, not topple him.

Even officials close to Mobutu's crumbling rule say the six million Shabans, hungry for change after 32 years of misrule, will mostly welcome Kabila with open arms if he advances further south in the province towards the capital.

The group of officers, while speaking for themselves, claimed all their fellow gendarmes now felt the same way -- despite having vowed to fight Kabila, branded a Rwandan agent, when his rebellion began last October in eastern Zaire.
"Before we thought it was Rwanda but now we think they are fighting for a cause," one officer said on Friday of the rebels whose startling advances have pushed them deep into Shaba.

The change of heart is no surprise. Today, Kabila looks like a winner and his disciplined fighters control about a quarter of the vast country. By contrast, Mobutu is stricken by cancer, his army has collapsed in the field and prominent members of his regime have sent their families abroad.
